full_judgment:
5. Defendant Nos. 11 and 12 contested the suit by filing joint written statement. Their contention is that Dhanobar and Nafar sold the suit land out and out to the defendants Nos. 4 and 5 by Kabala dated 26-2-52 (Exhibit 2) and the said deed was not a mortgage deed. It was an out and out sale deed and the allegation of returning the suit land by the defendant Nos. 4 and 5 is false and fabricated and the suit land has been accordingly recorded in the SA Khatian in the names of the defendants 4 and 5 correctly. Defendant No. 4 is Panchanan Pal and the defendant No. 5 is Santosh Kumar having migrated to India, the land was enlisted as enemy property. Defendant No. 11 is in possession of the suit land as lessee from the Government. 

 11. It is stated by the plaintiff that at the time of returning of the land Panchanan defendant No. 4 was present and he himself made the endorsement, but Santosh Kumar, the defendant No. 5 was not present at that time, and for that his father Surja Kanta Pal made the endorsement returning the land. The plaintiff further says that Santosh Pal was a minor and, as such, Surja Kanta Pal returned the land by the said endorsement, but nowhere in the Exhibit 2, it has been stated or referred that Santosh Pal was a minor and the document was executed and registered in the year 1952 and the endorsement as to reconveyance was made on 25th Chaitra, 1364 BS which would be in or around 1957 and even in the endorsement itself, there is no mention that Santosh was a minor and his father Surja Kanta Pal was in any manner authorised to make the endorsement reconveying the suit land, as alleged. 

 14. It is a dispute involving the point of law more than facts, to be decided whether the transfer by Exhibit 2 was a mortgage which took place in the year 1952 before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in and whether by alleged endorsement the suit land could be legally reconveyed. The endorsement seems to be a doubtful and not a genuine one. The suit land cannot be returned to the seller treating the transfer as a mortgage, in the manner as brought by the plaintiff. 

 15. Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act defines mortgagors of different kinds. The recitals of the Exhibit 2 in any manner does not contain any statements that the transferor is a mortgage. So, the transfer in question cannot be treated as a mortgage or even from the endorsement, it cannot be said that it was a mortgage and there is no separate deed of agreement to reconvey the suit land treating the transfer as a mortgage. Thus the transfer cannot be brought within the arena of the definition of a mortgage of any kind as embodied in section 58 of the Transfer of the Property Act. 

 Mr Habibul Alam, the learned Counsel for the appellant, tries to convince this Court that section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was applicable in this case and, as such, although there is no written agreement to reconvey the suit land but reconveyance of the same was made after enforcement of section 95(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and; as such, it was a legal and genuine one. Thus submission has no legal force because the transfer took place in the year 1952 before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in the locality and hence as there is no agreement there is no application of section 95 or 95(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in this legal conflict.
